title: Lantern Night
subtitle: Camp Pinecrest, Lantern Lake, Larkin Township, Pennsylvania, 16 to 19 September 1977

listing.title: Lantern Night 🛶
listing.blurb: The Poconos, September 1977. Camp Pinecrest, "a summer camp for grown-ups" since 1934, has had its last season. The lake is sold, the canoes are stacked, and the old staff have come back for one closing weekend and one last Lantern Night on the dock. Somebody in a carved wooden mask is walking the shore with an ice pike. By morning the road is under water, the phone line is cut, and nobody's car will start. The man in the mask is not the worst thing at Lantern Lake. He may be the only one who knows what is. Levels 3–5.

synopsis: Camp Pinecrest stands on the Neck, a wooded peninsula on the south shore of Lantern Lake in the Pocono Mountains of northeastern Pennsylvania, forty minutes north of Stroudsburg. It was a summer camp for grown-ups, never for anyone younger: from 1934 to 1977 office clerks, shop assistants, nurses, typists and factory hands from Philadelphia, Newark and New York came for a week of canoeing, tennis, square dances and the Saturday revue in the Playhouse, eighteen and over, as the first brochure said. Before that the lake belonged to the Lantern Lake Ice Company, whose cutters harvested its black winter ice from 1881 until refrigeration ruined them in 1932, and whose night gangs never looked into open water by lantern light without a hood over their faces. Pinecrest kept the habit as a custom: on Lantern Night, the last Friday of every season, the guests set paper lanterns afloat from the dock wearing carved wooden masks, "so the lake keeps no faces." In 1962 the director called the masks morbid and left them in the box. In 1977 the camp has been sold to a developer, the sale closes on Monday morning, and its owner, the man everyone has called Coach for fifteen years, has invited the old staff back for a closing weekend and one last Lantern Night, without the masks. The caretaker, Alvin Dreher, tried to hand them out and was sent away. Now he walks the shore at night in one of them with an ice pike, and in the small hours of Saturday morning he kills a man on the swimming dock. The rain has put the Outlet over the only bridge; the phone line has been cut at the pole; somebody has pulled the rotor from every distributor in the parking lot. The party, a township police officer, a nurse, a reporter, a folklorist, the developer's watchman and a counselor who was on the dock in 1962, are shut in on the Neck with a killer in a mask until the water goes down. But the thing in the lake is real. The cutters called it Old Glass. It wears the face of anyone it has seen in still water or a dark window at night, it cannot say that person's name, and a photograph shows it with no face at all. If it wears one face from dusk to dawn, and is carried over running water before the next dusk, it takes that person's life, flesh and name and all, and the person goes down into the lake in its place, faceless, to wait for a face of their own. That is what happened to the waterfront director, Curtis Seeley, in 1962. The man who has been living Curtis's life ever since, who never says his own name and has taken every mirror out of his house, is not Curtis Seeley. He is Lorenz Garside, an ice cutter taken by the lake in January 1914, and he has brought everybody back this weekend to give Old Glass somebody else's face. Over one long weekend and four scenarios, the closing party and Lantern Night, the first death and the cut line, the old camp records and the truth, and the last night before the water goes down, the party must survive the man in the mask, learn the rules of the thing he is hunting, find out who Coach really is, and call the drowned man in the lake by his own name.
hook: Friday 16 September 1977, about four in the afternoon. The road from Larkin Corners runs four miles through second-growth hemlock and laurel, crosses the Outlet on a concrete bridge beside a little shingled gatehouse, passes a stone dam and a huge windowless stone building with ICE painted on it in letters gone pink with age, and comes out on a gravel lot above the water. There are eleven cars in the lot: a Suburban with PINECREST on the door, a Plymouth Fury with a light bar, a Ridgeview Leisure Communities pickup, a Beetle, a Ford Pinto, a Pennsylvania Game Commission truck. Below the lot is the camp: a long stone Lodge with a porch, a dining hall, a white Playhouse, twenty little green cabins along the shore, a boathouse, and a long L-shaped dock running out into Lantern Lake, which is very still and very dark and reflects the hills on the far side so perfectly that it is hard to tell where the land stops. A hand-painted banner over the Lodge porch reads THANK YOU PINECREST 1934–1977, and from somewhere inside a piano is playing a song that was popular when Eisenhower was president. A woman in her forties with reading glasses on a chain comes up the path with a clipboard, says, "You made it. I'm Opal. Coach is down at the boathouse. Supper's at six-thirty, Lantern Night's at nine, and please, whatever you do, don't miss Winnie's pie." You are here because Pinecrest asked for you, or because something here has been asking for a long time. Opal wrote to the old staff. A reporter's editor wants the last weekend at the last grown-ups' camp in the Poconos. A folklorist wants the ice company's papers in the office attic. The developer needs a watchman from Monday. The township sent its one officer, because a guest who came early saw a man in a carved wooden mask standing at the end of the dock on Thursday night, and he did not answer when she called to him.

setting.name: Camp Pinecrest and Lantern Lake, Larkin Township, Pennsylvania, 16 to 19 September 1977
setting.description: Camp Pinecrest, Lantern Lake, the Lantern Lake Ice Company, Larkin Township, Larkin Corners and Ridgeview Leisure Communities are fictional. The Poconos, the ice industry and the 1970s second-home boom are real. From the 1880s to the 1930s Pocono lakes were harvested every winter for ice, cut in blocks by gangs with saws, tongs and hooks, stored in sawdust in great windowless icehouses, and shipped by rail to Philadelphia and New York, until electric refrigeration ended the trade almost overnight. From the 1920s to the 1960s the same mountains were full of resorts and camps for working adults from the cities, places with lakes, dance halls and theatres where a secretary from Newark could spend a week canoeing and see a revue on Saturday night; by the 1970s most of them were failing, and developers were buying them up for vacation-home subdivisions with names like Lakes and Estates. Camp Pinecrest is one of the last. It stands on the Neck, a sixty-acre peninsula of hemlock and white pine between Lantern Lake, a hundred and forty acres of cold, spring-fed water, on three sides, and on the fourth the Outlet, the stream that pours out over the ice company's old stone dam, under the camp road bridge and away south through a laurel marsh. The only road in or out crosses that bridge. Larkin Corners, four miles away, has a store, a church, a gas station, a firehouse and a payphone; Stroudsburg is forty minutes south. This weekend the remnants of a tropical storm come up the coast and stall over the mountains: rain from late Friday night until Sunday afternoon, the Outlet out of its banks and over the bridge by Saturday morning, and the road washed out at the Hemlock Run culvert half a mile beyond. The camp's one telephone line runs on poles beside that road. It is 1977: a gallon of gas is sixty-two cents, a Polaroid SX-70 pack of ten pictures costs about seven dollars, everyone smokes, the Lodge has a color television that gets two channels, the cars are Pintos, Novas, a Beetle and a Fury, and every one of them has a distributor under the hood whose rotor can be pulled in five seconds by someone who knows engines.
setting.atmosphere: Off-season melancholy turning to siege. Pinecrest at the end is a sweet, shabby, much-loved place full of people who were young here: the old bandleader at the Lodge piano, the arts counselor with her slide carousel, the cook who has made the same pie for thirty-one summers, the nurse, the drama counselor who left in 1962 and never came back. Let the players enjoy them. Then let the lake do the work. Lantern Lake is the stillest water in the mountains, and at night it is a black mirror; the horror of this campaign is reflections, faces and names. Show it sideways: a reflection that is a beat late, wet footprints that come up out of the lake and stop at a dry door, a friend's voice at the Lodge door asking to be let in while that friend is sitting beside you, a Polaroid that develops with a grey smear where a face should be, a man who has been dead since one in the morning walking along the cabins at dusk with his hands in his pockets. The man in the mask is the slasher the players expect, and he should be frightening: silent, strong, always ahead of them, the carved face with a painted lantern on its brow appearing in a window the party passed. Let them fear him first. The slow turn is that he is a grieving, guilty, certain old man who knows the lake's rules and has made a terrible mistake, and that the kindly host is the one to fear. Violence is quick and paperback-plain: a blow, a fall, a body under a tarp. Rain on the roof all weekend. The light goes out once.

regions.name: The Gate and the Outlet
regions.description: Where the camp road crosses the Outlet: a concrete bridge of 1936 with iron pipe railings, the little shingled gatehouse beside it where the camp kept its sign-in book, and the telephone pole by the gatehouse where the camp's line comes in. Upstream is the stone dam of 1881, forty yards long, with a spillway where the lake slides over in a smooth black sheet and falls ten feet into the Outlet. The Outlet itself is a fast stream twenty feet wide in a stony bed, knee-deep in a dry September and, from Saturday morning, a brown torrent over the bridge deck. It is running water: the boundary of everything that happens on the Neck.

regions.name: The Ice Company Ground
regions.description: Between the dam and the camp: the Icehouse, a stone-and-timber building of 1881, three storeys high and windowless, with walls two feet thick and sawdust still in the corners, where Pinecrest stores its canoes in winter; the caretaker's cottage, a small frame house by the dam where Alvin Dreher has lived since 1946; the Office, the ice company's clapboard counting house of 1881, now the camp office, with the ice company's papers in the attic; and on the knoll above the dam, the Cutters' Ground, a burying ground inside a low iron fence where the ice company buried its men from 1884 to 1951.

regions.name: The Camp
regions.description: The Lodge, the ice company's stone bunkhouse of 1881, rebuilt in 1934: a long building with a porch on the lake side, a great stone fireplace, a lounge with the piano and the television, twelve guest rooms upstairs, and in every doorway the ice company's iron sill plates, worn bright by ninety years of boots. The Dining Hall, attached to the Lodge by a covered walk, with its long tables, Winnie's kitchen and, along one wall, forty-three framed staff photographs, one for every season. The Playhouse, white clapboard, 1938, two hundred seats and a stage. The Director's House, a big log cabin on the point, where Coach lives. Birch Row, twenty green frame cabins along the east shore, built from 1934 to 1950, two beds each, screen doors, wooden sills.

regions.name: The Waterfront
regions.description: The Boathouse, a long shingled building over the water with a workshop at the back, canoes on racks, rowboats, the ice company's old flat workboat and, under the floor, a covered slip of black water where Old Glass lies by day. The swimming dock, an L of grey planks a hundred feet out and fifty across, with iron lantern posts every ten feet, the place where Lantern Night is held. The beach, a strip of hauled-in sand. Across the water, two thirds of a mile away, the north shore: dark woods, a brook coming in, nothing else.

regions.name: Lantern Lake
regions.description: A hundred and forty acres of deep, cold, spring-fed water, sixty feet deep off the point, so clear that on a still day you can see the old cutting channels' log booms lying on the bottom, and so still at night that it reflects the stars. It does not freeze any more the way it did for the cutters; the winters are not what they were. Sound carries across it. Nobody at Pinecrest has swum in it after dark since 1962.

regions.name: Larkin Corners and Beyond
regions.description: Four miles from the gate by road: a crossroads with Kunkle's store, a white church, a gas station, the volunteer firehouse and a payphone. The township's police office is one room in the firehouse. Stroudsburg, the county seat, is forty minutes south, with the courthouse, the hospital, the newspaper and the State Police barracks. From Saturday morning until early Monday, all of it is on the far side of the flooded Outlet.

campaignRules.name: The Closing Weekend Clock
campaignRules.description: The campaign runs from Friday afternoon to Monday morning, and things happen on time whether or not the players are watching. Tell the players the day and the hour whenever they ask. pc-scenario-001 is Friday 16 September (arrival, supper, Lantern Night at 9 p.m.); pc-scenario-002 is Saturday 17 (the body at dawn, the flood, the cut line, the first night of the siege); pc-scenario-003 is Sunday 18 (the records, the truth, the boat on the Outlet); pc-scenario-004 is Sunday night to Monday dawn (the last night). ALREADY DONE: on Tuesday 13 September Coach bought a spare distributor rotor at an auto parts store in Stroudsburg (the receipt is in his desk). On Thursday night Bev Kleinfelter saw a man in a mask at the end of the dock. IF NOBODY INTERFERES: Friday 9 p.m., Lantern Night without masks; Coach asks Gene Marcotte to light the first lantern and look into the water; Old Glass rises and borrows Gene's face. 10:30 p.m. the rain begins; Alvin pulls every rotor in the lot. 11:45 p.m. 'Gene' is seen on the dock while Gene is in the Lodge. Saturday 1:10 a.m. Alvin kills the real Gene on the dock, believing him to be the thing. 4 a.m. Alvin cuts the phone line at the gatehouse pole. 6:20 a.m. Winnie finds the body. By 10 a.m. the Outlet is over the bridge. 7:40 p.m. dusk: 'Gene' walks along Birch Row; at 1 a.m. Sunday the borrowed face fails (a day since it saw him alive). Saturday 11 p.m. Old Glass, wearing Santi Rivera's face, knocks at the Lodge door. Sunday: rain until 2 p.m.; at 3 p.m. Coach tries to row 'Santi' across the flooded Outlet below the dam and is driven back; at dusk he takes the real Santi down to the dock with a lantern 'to check the boats', lets the lake see his face, and locks him in the Icehouse 'for his own safety'. Sunday night Old Glass wears Santi unnamed from dusk to dawn. Monday 5 a.m. the water is off the bridge; 6:15 a.m. Coach puts his spare rotor in the Suburban and drives 'Santi' over the Outlet; Santi goes down into the lake, and Curtis Seeley drives away in Santi's life. The sale closes at 10 a.m. If Coach's chosen face is lost, he chooses again: the loneliest person on the Neck, often a player character.

campaignRules.name: Old Glass: Its Rules (GM only)
campaignRules.description: GM ONLY until the players learn each one; never change a rule once it is learned. Old Glass is the thing in Lantern Lake, and it follows five rules, each with at least three clues (controlFile.clues). RULE ONE, THE CALL: it rises only when a face looks into the still water of Lantern Lake by lantern light or firelight after dark; once risen it stays up until it takes a life or is laid. It can wear the face and voice of any living person it has seen, in the lake or in a dark window near the lake at night, within the last day; when the day runs out, that face fails and it needs another. If the person dies, it can go on wearing the dead face until the day runs out, but there is no life in it to take. A masked or covered face it cannot see, and cannot borrow. RULE TWO, THE TELL: wearing a face, it cannot speak that person's name, and a mirror, a dark window or a photograph shows it with no face at all, only grey. Whoever has taken a life through the lake carries the same tells for the rest of that life: no face in a mirror or a photograph, and never the name of the one whose life they took. RULE THREE, THE BOUNDS: it cannot cross running water unless it is carried, in a boat, a car or someone's arms; the Outlet is its wall. It cannot cross a threshold with iron in it unless the person whose face it wears invites it in. It sleeps by day in the water under the Boathouse, and comes out by day only to be carried. RULE FOUR, THE TRADE: if it wears one living person's face from dusk to dawn, and that person has not looked it in the eyes and told it their own name, and it is carried over running water before the next dusk, it becomes that person in flesh, memory and life, and the person goes down into the lake in its place, faceless, as the next Old Glass. A person who looks it in the eyes and says their own name aloud takes their face back for good: it can never wear that face again, and it falls into lake water and weed until the next dusk. RULE FIVE, THE REST: every Old Glass was once a person the lake kept. Called by its own full name, to its face, by someone who knew it in life, it remembers who it was, and walks back into the lake and lies down for good, and the chain ends. The one in the lake now is Curtis Seeley. A wrong name does nothing, and it knows you tried: it will want the speaker's face next.

campaignRules.name: Rites That Work Here
campaignRules.description: Rites work only because Old Glass's rules say so (dread.json rites_and_wards); anyone can try them, an Occultist does them better, and they do nothing against Alvin Dreher, who is a man. THE MASK: any mask, hood, scarf or cloth over the face by the water at night keeps Old Glass from seeing that face (Rule One); the Pinecrest masks in the cedar box are only good ones, carved by the founder in 1934. Drawn curtains on lakeside windows at night do the same. THE IRON SILL: iron set across a doorway bars it unless the person it is copying invites it in; the Lodge's ice-company sill plates already do this, and an ice pike, tongs, a crowbar, a fire iron or a row of nails laid across a cabin's wooden sill works for as long as it lies there (Rule Three). THE MIRROR: a hand mirror, a dark window or a Polaroid shows it faceless; a picture develops in about a minute (Rule Two). RUNNING WATER: it will not cross the Outlet, a brook, or a garden hose left running across a path, unless carried. NAMING YOURSELF: the person whose face it wears looks it in the eyes and says their own full name aloud; that face is theirs for good (Rule Four). It takes nerve: a fear check against the truth of it, DC 20, or DC 18 if they know the rule, and on a failure they cannot get the words out this round. THE TRUE NAME: someone who knew the drowned man looks it in the eyes and says 'Curtis Seeley' aloud, Opal, Winnie, Nell or Odessa, or anyone holding something of his and his own story (an Occult check DC 15 to say it so it hears, advantage for those who knew him); it lays Old Glass to rest (Rule Five). WRONG RITES: salt, prayer, holy water, burning the masks, silver, fire, dynamite in the lake; nothing happens, and it knows you tried. Iron weapons hurt it fully; ordinary weapons do half. Dropping it to 0 only puts it back in the lake until the next dusk.

campaignRules.name: Dread at Lantern Lake
campaignRules.description: Use dread.json. Fear checks (WIS saves) in this campaign: DC 10 for a sign (wet footprints coming up from the lake and stopping at a dry door; pondweed on a cabin step; a reflection a beat late; frost on the inside of a boathouse window in September; a friend's voice where that friend cannot be); DC 15 for seeing it (someone you know standing on the dock in the rain while they sit beside you; a dead man walking along Birch Row at dusk; the man in the mask in a window you just passed); DC 20 for the truth (a Polaroid that develops with no face; a body that runs out of its clothes as lake water; Coach's face missing from fifteen staff photographs; your own face looking back at you from the lake while you stand on the dock). Knowing one of Old Glass's rules lowers the DC by 2. Darkness adds 2. The same horror costs Dread once per scene. The man in the mask is an ordinary terror: seeing him is DC 13 the first time each scene, and a Skeptic's Debunker or There's an Explanation applies to him fully. Recovery as dread.json: the Lodge fireplace with company, a long night's sleep, Winnie's coffee and pie, a drink at the Lodge bar, Marvin playing the piano. At Pinecrest a long rest is hard to come by: nobody sleeps soundly on Saturday or Sunday night. Once per scenario the light goes out at the worst moment: the camp's power comes from one line on the same poles as the phone, and there is a generator in the Icehouse that has to be started by hand.

campaignRules.name: The Man in the Mask (GM only)
campaignRules.description: GM ONLY until the players learn it. The man in the carved mask is Alvin Dreher, 58, the caretaker, a man, not a monster: use the Masked Killer (adversaries.json) with the changes in controlFile.suspects. He knows Rules One, Two and Three from his father's notes, and half of Rule Four; he does not know Rule Five and does not believe the thing can be ended. He believes only two things will hold it: no masks off by the water, and nothing carried over the Outlet. So he pulled the rotors, cut the phone, guards the bridge and the boats, and kills whatever he believes is wearing a stolen face, which only puts it back in the lake until dusk, and which on Saturday morning was the real Gene Marcotte. He cannot tell the thing from a person any better than the players can; his test is a dark window or a hand mirror, and in the rain at night he guesses. He will attack anyone he believes is the thing, anyone trying to cross the Outlet with someone else, and anyone who tries to take the mask off him. He will not hurt Winnie Szot or Opal Seeley, and either of them can talk him down (the Masked Killer's 'A Person': a Persuasion check DC 13 with proof that they know what he knows, or DC 10 if they say his name and his father's). Captured or talked down, he tells the truth as he knows it, the 1914 log, the 1962 ride he gave 'Curtis' over the bridge, and what Coach is, and he wants to be arrested afterwards. He has nothing to do with illness; he is grieving, guilty and certain, and he is wrong about almost everything except the lake.

campaignRules.name: Grown-Ups Only
campaignRules.description: Pinecrest was always an adults' camp, eighteen and over, and nobody in this campaign, past or present, is a child: no campers, no young guests, no child victims, no child ghosts, no backstory involving anyone's children. If a player asks, the answer is that Pinecrest never took them. Every person Old Glass has kept was a grown man. Violence is quick and plain, a paperback ghost story's level: a blow, a fall, a body under a tarp, never lingered on; nothing lurid between anyone, ever; no animal is harmed. Nobody here is ill and nobody escaped from anywhere: Alvin is a grieving man with a terrible certainty, and Dread is fright, not illness. Old Glass belongs to no people, church or tradition; it is the lake's, and the ice cutters' name for it is only a name. Before the first scene, ask the players what they do not want in the game, and honour 'skip that' at any time, at once, by cutting away or fading out (dread.json running_horror). The most likely things to need it are drowning, a body under water, and being shut in the dark.

explorationRules: This is a siege on a clock in one small place, and the map is a schematic of it: the camp in the middle of the Neck, the lake on three sides, the dam, the Icehouse and the gate to the south-east, and the Outlet between the party and everything else. Nothing on the Neck is more than ten minutes' walk from anything else; the Director's House on the point is the farthest. The unit of time is the hour, and the Closing Weekend Clock (campaignRules) is the engine: Old Glass, Alvin and Coach all act on it. By day the party can go anywhere; after dusk, every trip between buildings is a scene, in the rain, by flashlight. From Saturday morning nobody drives out (no rotors, and the bridge under water) and nobody telephones (the line is cut at the gatehouse pole, and the township cruiser's radio is in a dead spot under the ridge). A strong swimmer with a rope can get across the flooded Outlet below the bridge by day (Athletics DC 18, 2d6 bludgeoning on a failure and swept fifty yards down), and a party that does it reaches Larkin Corners in two hours on foot and can bring the State Police back by Monday noon, after the last night; let them try, and let it cost. The investigation follows the three-clue rule (dread.json investigation, and Old Glass's Rules): core clues are found by anyone who looks in the right place; rolls add detail and speed, never dead ends. Fights are rare, short and frightening, and most of them are against Alvin in the dark or Old Glass at a door. Money is 1977 dollars: a cup of coffee is a quarter, a pack of cigarettes sixty cents, gas sixty-two cents a gallon, a Polaroid pack of ten pictures about seven dollars, a week at Pinecrest in its best years forty-five dollars with meals, and Ridgeview is paying $410,000 for the Neck and the lake.

controlFile.note: The fixed truth of the campaign, for the GM only. It does not change because a player has a more exciting theory, and Old Glass's rules never change once learned. Camp Pinecrest, Lantern Lake, the Neck, the Lantern Lake Ice Company, Larkin Township, Larkin Corners, Ridgeview Leisure Communities and every person in the campaign are fictional. The Pocono Mountains, the natural-ice trade and its collapse, the adults' resort camps of the mid-century Poconos, the 1970s vacation-home boom, Stroudsburg, the Polaroid SX-70 and the fetch of British and Irish folklore (a double that appears to the living) are real. Old Glass belongs to no religion, people or tradition; the ice cutters' name for it is a work name. Pinecrest was always an adults' camp: nobody in this campaign, at any date, is a child.
controlFile.theTruth: Lantern Lake keeps people. Nobody knows how long it has: the oldest cutters said it had always been so. Now and then a man is lost in the lake and never found, and the lake keeps him: he becomes Old Glass, a faceless thing in the black water that wants a face and a life to leave in. When a face looks into the still lake by lantern light after dark, it rises and borrows that face, and if it can wear one face through a night unnamed and be carried over running water before the next dusk, it takes that person's life, flesh, memory and name, and walks away as them; the person goes down into the lake in its place and becomes the next Old Glass. The Lantern Lake Ice Company's men learned the rules the hard way. In the winter of 1887 a cutter named Mathias Kintner went through the ice and was never found. In January 1888 something came up out of a night channel wearing the face of a young cutter on the gang, and would not say his name, and the foreman, Gottlob Brodt, who had known Mathias Kintner twenty years and knew him in the way it stood, called it 'Mathias Kintner' to its face, and it went down into the cut and was never seen again, and the lake was quiet for twenty-five years. In December 1913 a cutter who had signed on under a false name, and whose real name nobody ever learned, went through the ice at night and was not found. In January 1914 his Old Glass rose in a night channel and borrowed the face of Lorenz Garside, 27, a cutter from Larkin Corners, and the next morning 'Lorenz' rode out over the Outlet trestle on the ice train, and Lorenz Garside went down into the lake. The superintendent, Rudolph Dreher, wrote it in the night log, and from then on the night gangs worked hooded, and the lake kept nothing for forty-eight years. The thing wearing Lorenz's life lived quietly in Larkin Corners, never once said its own name, and was buried in the Cutters' Ground in 1951 as LORENZ GARSIDE; its own true name is lost. In 1933 the ice company failed, and Philomena Delamater, a Philadelphia store's personnel director, bought the Neck for a summer camp for working adults. Rudolph Dreher stayed on as caretaker and told her the rules, and she made them a custom: Lantern Night, the last Friday of every season, lanterns on the water and a carved mask on every face. His son Alvin took over as caretaker in 1946, after the war, and kept the masks. In 1962 the new director, Herbert Amsel, called the masks morbid and left them in the box. That night the waterfront director, Curtis Seeley, 30, the best swimmer Pinecrest ever had, a Korea veteran and a kind, joking, well-liked man, leaned out over the dock with his lantern and looked a long time into the water, and Old Glass, which was Lorenz Garside, rose and borrowed his face. At midnight Curtis took his last canoe paddle of the season, as he always did. At seven the next morning 'Curtis' asked Alvin Dreher for a ride into Larkin Corners, and Alvin, who did not know yet, drove him over the Outlet bridge. Curtis Seeley's canoe was found drifting empty at noon. 'Curtis' came back on Monday, said he had left it untied, and left Pinecrest with everyone else. The man who has lived as Curtis Seeley since is Lorenz Garside, born in 1886, an ice cutter who spent forty-eight years faceless in the dark. He never says the name Curtis Seeley; he made everyone call him Coach, and signs C.S. He cannot swim and will not go near the water ('the shoulder'). His handwriting is the copperplate of a 1900s schoolroom, not Curtis's square print. He appears in no photograph and no mirror with a face, and has taken every mirror out of the Director's House and painted its lakeside windows. And since 1962, in every dark window anywhere, he has seen a man with no face standing just behind his own reflection, looking for its own face: the real Curtis, in the lake. In 1965 he bought Pinecrest with Curtis's inheritance and kept Alvin on, and the two of them have kept a silent truce for twelve years: Alvin handed out the masks every Lantern Night, Coach allowed it, and the faceless man stayed in the water. Pinecrest has lost money every year since 1968. This summer Coach sold the Neck to Ridgeview Leisure Communities, which will drain the lake down for a beach and build three hundred vacation houses, and he cannot face leaving with the faceless man behind him in every window. So he has planned a closing weekend: the old staff, a last Lantern Night, no masks, and a stranger to light the first lantern. If Old Glass takes someone else's life and walks away in it, Curtis Seeley will be somebody else, and the next thing in the lake will have no claim on him. He has a spare rotor for the Suburban because he knew Alvin would pull the others. He does not want anyone dead. He only wants someone gone.
suspects: 'Coach', the man known as Curtis Seeley, 45 by his face, owner and director of Camp Pinecrest: THE ONE WHO RAISED IT. In truth Lorenz Garside, ice cutter, born 1886, taken by the lake in January 1914, living Curtis Seeley's life since September 1962. Big, sun-browned, genial, with a whistle on a lanyard he never blows, a cardigan, a booming welcome and a habit of calling everyone 'friend' or 'pal', because he cannot say 'Curtis' and avoids names generally. He chose Gene Marcotte as the face; when Gene dies he chooses the loneliest person on the Neck (Santi Rivera by default, or a player character who has been alone at a dark window). His plan: keep the chosen person away from Old Glass so they cannot name themselves to it (at dusk on Sunday he takes Santi down to the dock with a lantern so the lake sees his face, then locks him in the Icehouse 'for his safety, with Alvin out there'), then drive the thing over the bridge at dawn on Monday with his spare rotor. Night Watchman statistics with a Service revolver from the office safe, and he will use it only on Alvin. Turnable: by Opal, by the 1913 payroll signature put in front of him, by being made to look into a dark window with the party watching. He can save himself at any moment by looking Old Glass in the eyes, if it wears his face, and saying his own true name, 'Lorenz Garside', aloud; that is the one thing in the world he is most afraid to do. THIS IS WHAT SUCCEEDS IF NOBODY INTERFERES: at 6:15 on Monday morning the Suburban crosses the Outlet, Santi Rivera goes down into the lake, and Curtis Seeley drives away in his life.

Alvin Dreher, 58, caretaker since 1946, son of the ice superintendent Rudolph Dreher: THE MAN IN THE MASK. A big, quiet, weather-cut man in a wool shirt, a war veteran (Italy, 1944), who has lived alone in the cottage by the dam for thirty-one years and fixed every pipe, roof and motor on the Neck. He knows the rules from his father's notebook and the night log, and has believed them since 1962, when he gave 'Curtis' the ride over the bridge; he found the empty canoe himself, and he has never forgiven himself. On Friday he tried to hand out the masks and Coach sent him off in front of everyone. He put on the mask himself (Philomena's 1934 carving with the lantern painted on its brow) and he will not take it off by the water. He pulled the rotors (they are in a coffee can in the cottage's woodbox), cut the phone line, and at 1:10 on Saturday morning killed Gene Marcotte on the dock with an ice pike, believing him to be the thing; he saw two Genes that night and struck the wrong one, and he knew it when the body did not run to water. Masked Killer statistics (adversaries.json) with these changes: Blade is an ice pike, a long ash pole with a forged iron spike, piercing rather than slashing, same numbers (iron: it hurts Old Glass fully); Gets Back Up and Always Ahead as written (he knows every path, crawlspace and boathouse door on the Neck); 'A Person': Winnie or Opal can talk him down (campaignRules, The Man in the Mask). He wants to be stopped. He also wants, more than anything, for nothing to cross that bridge.

Old Glass, which is Curtis Seeley: THE THING IN THE LAKE. Not a villain. A drowned man who has forgotten most of himself in fifteen years of black water and wants a face, any face, and most of all his own. It does not hate anyone. It will strike, with cold hands, anyone who stands between it and a car, a boat, the water or its own face, and it will use any voice it has borrowed to get through a door. See controlFile.oldGlass.
redHerrings: The man in the mask is the killer, and the killer is the threat. Both half true. Alvin killed Gene, and he will hurt someone else if he guesses wrong, but he is trying to keep the thing in, and the party should end up needing what he knows.

Ridgeview Leisure Communities. A developer buying a beloved camp to drain the lake: the players will suspect Ridgeview, or Gene, of something. Gene Marcotte was exactly what he seemed, a surveyor from Allentown with a wife in Emmaus and a bad back, and the company has never heard of Old Glass.

Lorenz Garside's grave. The stone in the Cutters' Ground reads LORENZ GARSIDE 1886–1951, and the players may think the thing in the lake is Lorenz, or that the grave holds the answer. The grave holds the nameless cutter of 1913 who lived as Lorenz. Its true name is lost; saying 'Lorenz Garside' to Old Glass does nothing, because the one in the lake now is Curtis.

Nell Sorensen. She was on the dock in 1962, she left the next day and never came back, and she makes her living reading people on a stage. If anyone has a secret, the players will think it is her. Her secret is only that she saw Curtis's reflection fail to move, and ran.

A drowning ghost or a revenant. The dead man walking on Saturday evening looks like a revenant, and the wet footprints look like a drowned one. It is neither; salt, burial rites and fire do nothing (Rites That Work).
clues: A. THE MAN IN THE MASK IS ALVIN DREHER, AND HE IS HUNTING SOMETHING ELSE. A1: Alvin with the cedar mask box at the dock on Friday, sent away by Coach, and Philomena's carved mask missing from it afterwards (pc-scenario-001). A2: the rotors in a coffee can in the cottage woodbox and the hacksaw at the gatehouse pole (pc-scenario-002). A3: Gene's wound is from an ice pike, and Alvin's rack has an empty peg (pc-scenario-002). A4: Winnie: 'Alvin Dreher never hurt a living soul. Not one he knew was living' (pc-scenario-002). A5: the man in the mask holds a hand mirror up to people before he strikes (pc-scenario-002).

B. SOMETHING IS WEARING PEOPLE'S FACES. B1: 'Gene' on the dock at 11:45 p.m. Friday while Gene was in the Lodge (pc-scenario-001). B2: 'Gene' walking on Birch Row at dusk on Saturday, twelve hours after Odessa pronounced him dead (pc-scenario-002). B3: wet footprints that come up out of the lake and stop at the Lodge door; pondweed on the iron sill (pc-scenario-002). B4: a voice at the Lodge door, Santi's, asking to be let in while Santi sits by the fire (pc-scenario-002). B5: Paula's Polaroids from Lantern Night: one 'Gene' on the dock with a grey smear for a face (pc-scenario-001, developed in pc-scenario-002).

C. ITS RULES. C1 (the call and the mask): Rudolph Dreher's night log, January 1914: 'no man to look on open water by lantern unhooded'; Philomena's 1934 Lantern Night card, 'so the lake keeps no faces'; Winnie's memory; Zachary's interview with the last Lantern Lake cutter (pc-scenario-001, pc-scenario-003). C2 (the tell): the Polaroids; the mirror Alvin carries; the 1914 log, 'Garside will not say his name' (pc-scenario-002, pc-scenario-003). C3 (the bounds): the thing never crosses the flooded Outlet on its own; the log's note on the ice train; the Lodge's iron sills keep it out while Birch Row's do not (pc-scenario-002, pc-scenario-003). C4 (the trade): the 1914 log, 'Garside rode out on the morning ice train, and the lake was quiet'; Alvin's 1962 ride; Opal's account of the canoe (pc-scenario-003). C5 (the rest): the 1888 log entry, foreman Gottlob Brodt calling 'Mathias Kintner' to its face; Philomena's letter to Winnie, 'if you ever see a face on the water you know, call it by its name, poor soul'; The Thin Place at the dock (pc-scenario-003).

D. COACH IS NOT CURTIS SEELEY. D1: he never says his own name, and Opal has not heard him say it in fifteen years (pc-scenario-001). D2: in every staff photograph from 1965 to 1976 Coach's face is a grey blur, 'he can't stand still for a picture' (pc-scenario-001). D3: no mirrors in the Director's House, lakeside windows painted over (pc-scenario-003). D4: Curtis's letters from 1952 to 1962 are in square print; Coach writes copperplate, and so did whoever signed LORENZ GARSIDE on the ice company's 1913 payroll (pc-scenario-003). D5: the champion swimmer will not go near the water; he holds an ice pike like a cutter (pc-scenario-001, pc-scenario-002). D6: Alvin's account of 1962 (pc-scenario-003).

E. COACH RAISED IT ON PURPOSE AND MEANS TO CARRY IT OUT. E1: he left the masks in the box and asked Gene to light the first lantern and look (pc-scenario-001). E2: the auto parts receipt for a rotor dated 13 September, before anything happened (pc-scenario-003). E3: the rowboat on the flooded Outlet on Sunday with 'Santi' in it (pc-scenario-003). E4: the real Santi locked in the Icehouse (pc-scenario-004).

F. THE THING IN THE LAKE IS CURTIS SEELEY. F1: the chain in the log, Kintner, the nameless cutter, Garside, and the date of Curtis's empty canoe (pc-scenario-003). F2: The Thin Place or Old Lore at the dock: it wants its own face, and a name it cannot reach (pc-scenario-003). F3: Opal: 'Curtis could swim the lake end to end. Coach can't swim a stroke' (pc-scenario-003). F4: once it has worn Coach's face, it comes to the Director's House (pc-scenario-004).

oldGlass.name: Old Glass (the thing in Lantern Lake)
oldGlass.basis: A unique campaign creature. Use The Fetch (adversaries.json) with these changes, and remember it is less a monster to fight than a drowned man with rules.
oldGlass.appearance: By day, nothing: a darker patch in the water under the Boathouse. At night, whoever it is wearing, wet to the skin, hair flat, clothes the person was last seen in, walking with a slight wrongness, as if it were remembering how. Up close it is cold, it smells of the lake, and its eyes do not quite track a lantern. In a mirror, a dark window or a photograph, it is a man-shaped greyness with no face at all, like breath on glass. When it falls it runs out of its clothes as lake water and weed.
oldGlass.statistics: AC 12; 55 hit points; speed 30 ft, swim 40 ft. Resistant to bludgeoning, piercing and slashing from ordinary weapons; immune to cold and poison; vulnerable to iron (an ice pike, tongs, a crowbar, a fire iron or a shotgun loaded with nails does full damage and no resistance applies) and to its true name (Rule Five). Cold Hand: two attacks, +4 to hit, 2d6+2 cold damage; a creature hit by both in one turn while standing in water is pulled under (combat.json, grappled, escape DC 13). Wear Their Face: as The Fetch, but only faces it has seen in the lake or a dark window by the lake at night within the last day; DC 14 Insight to see something wrong in a friend, and then a fear check against the truth (DC 20). It cannot be destroyed by damage: at 0 hit points it runs out of its clothes as lake water and weed, loses the face it wore, and rises again at the next dusk. Fear: sign DC 10, seen DC 15, truth DC 20.
rules: Rises when a face looks into the still lake by lantern light after dark, and wears the face of anyone it has seen in the water or a dark window there within the last day
Can't speak the name of the person it copies; a mirror, a dark window or a photograph shows it with no face
Can't cross running water unless carried, or an iron threshold unless the one it copies invites it in
Laid to rest when someone who knew it in life calls it by its own name to its face
oldGlass.wantsAndWhy: It wants a face and a life to walk away in, and under that, its own face, which Coach is wearing. It remembers almost nothing: the feel of a canoe paddle, a sister's laugh, a song from 1958 that Marvin plays on Friday night, which makes it stand still on the dock in the rain to listen. It is not cruel. It is a man who has been in the dark for fifteen years, and it is desperate.

controlFile.theKeyClue: Everything turns on the night log of the Lantern Lake Ice Company, 1884 to 1932, in a tin trunk in the Office attic, and above all on two entries in Rudolph Dreher's hand: January 1888, the foreman calling 'Mathias Kintner' to its face, and January 1914, 'Garside will not say his name.' Point every early clue at the ice company (the masks, the Icehouse, Alvin's father, the cutters' graves, Zachary's thesis), and let Zachary or Opal be the door to the attic. If the party reaches pc-scenario-004 without the log, Alvin has the 1914 pages torn out and folded in his shirt pocket, and Winnie remembers what Philomena told her about calling it by its name.
controlFile.outcomes: There is no clean ending, only costs. THE NAME (the chain ends): someone who knew Curtis Seeley, Opal, Winnie, Nell or Odessa, looks Old Glass in the eyes and calls it 'Curtis Seeley', and it remembers; its borrowed face becomes, for one breath, Curtis's own, it says 'Opal?', and it walks down the dock into the lake and lies down, and Lantern Lake is only water ever after. Every character present drops to Dread 0. Coach can say the name Curtis Seeley for the first time in fifteen years, and his face comes back into mirrors; he is a ninety-one-year-old ice cutter in a stolen life, and what happens to him (a confession to Nolan, Opal's judgement, the sale) is the players' and his own. THE RETURN: Old Glass wears Coach's face from dusk to dawn and is carried over the Outlet; Curtis Seeley comes home after fifteen years in the lake, lost and shaking and forty-five, and Lorenz Garside goes back into the dark; Lantern Lake still keeps a man, and the developer is about to sell three hundred houses on its shore. COACH'S BARGAIN: the thing drives away in Santi's or a player character's life, and someone the party knows is in the lake; they know the rules now, and the name. ALVIN'S WAY: nothing crosses, the thing is put down every night until the masks go back on, and at dawn on Monday the State Police come over the bridge to a dead surveyor, a caretaker who confesses to it, and a lake that will be full of vacation-home windows next summer. In every ending, Alvin Dreher is a man who killed an innocent man in the dark, and says so.
